title: A son is born
hook: news of his son arrives; the child is named Rahula, "a fetter"
carry: love, and the fear inside it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth sight: a samana, a calm wanderer with a bowl. Your line was there is another way to live. Whose calm face did you find? Day thirty-five, the last day in the palace week.
screen: `SAMANA — THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: A messenger is hurrying down the road with news from the palace. In the stories, the prince is riding home from the park, the fourth sight still shining in his mind, when the messenger reaches him. Yasodhara has given birth. You have a son. New parents sometimes describe two things arriving at once: a love bigger than they expected, and right behind it, the fear of losing what they love. The prince, the stories say, answers with a strange sentence. Not a cheer. Something closer to a sigh. Today's word is the name that came from it.
screen: `A MESSENGER ON THE ROAD.` → `YOU HAVE A SON.` → `NOT A CHEER. A SIGH.`

segments.voice: What the prince says, in the later telling, is: a rahula is born, a fetter is born. A bond. Something that ties me down. When the king hears it, he names the baby Rahula. It sounds harsh to modern ears, and people read it in more than one way. Some hear a father torn: he has just glimpsed another way to live, and now there's a child holding him to this one. Others hear simple honesty about love. The prince doesn't say the baby is bad. He says the love is binding. And some scholars add a note: the name may once have meant something else, perhaps tied to Rahu, the shadow that swallows the moon in an eclipse, and the fetter story may explain a name that came first. The traditions also tell the timing differently. In the Pali commentaries, Rahula is born the day his father leaves. In some northern Buddhist tellings, he's born years later, on the night of the awakening. The sources disagree, and that's fine to say. What today's word holds is the feeling underneath. Love, and the fear inside it. Buddhism doesn't say stop loving. It says look closely at the gripping, the part that wants to hold so tight nothing can ever change. And Rahula doesn't vanish from the story. He comes back, and the Buddha himself will teach him. That's a story for later. Now look back at this week: three palaces, Yasodhara, four sights, and a son. Everything the prince has, and everything he is about to leave.
screen: `A RAHULA IS BORN — A FETTER.` · `A FATHER TORN, OR PLAIN HONESTY?` · `THE SOURCES DISAGREE.` · `LOVE WITHOUT GRIPPING.` · then, large: `LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Find something you love that you can hold: a mug, a photo, a stone from a beach, your own hand. Sit with it. Now close your fingers around it tightly. Feel the grip, the tension up the arm. Stay there a breath or two. Then slowly loosen. Let it rest in an open palm. Still yours, still loved, just not squeezed. Notice the difference in your body between holding and gripping. Breathe with the open hand. The bell holds the time.
Rahula. The Buddha's son, whose name, in the old telling, means a fetter: the tie of love that holds us.
Your line: love, and the fear inside it. Today, when you feel the worry that comes with loving someone, notice it, and loosen your grip by one finger. Day thirty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Rahula's birth as part of the going forth, and Buddhist parents are taught to love fully while practicing non-attachment, which means not clinging, rather than not caring.

original.note: Pali: the name of the Buddha's son, explained in the commentaries as a fetter or bond.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha called his baby a chain.
what it means: the name holds the honest truth that love binds us, and the fear of loss comes with it.
what a scholar hears: the Nidanakatha derives Rahula from rahu, a fetter; many scholars suspect a link to Rahu, the eclipse demon, with the fetter story explaining the name after the fact.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the news of Rahula's birth

notes: The prince's words 'a rahula is born, a fetter is born' are paraphrased from the Nidanakatha; confirm.

Timing traditions: Theravada commentaries (born the day of the going forth) vs. Mulasarvastivada/other northern accounts (a six-year pregnancy, born the night of the awakening). Confirm framing as 'some northern Buddhist tellings'.
The Rahu (eclipse) etymology is a scholarly suggestion, presented as 'may'. Confirm it's worth including.
